prompt: What does a React Native <Text> become on an Android phone?
hint: There is no browser in a React Native app.

choices.text: An HTML element inside a web view
choices.why: That is how some older frameworks worked; React Native draws native views.

choices.text: A native TextView
choices.why: Right. On iOS the same component becomes a UILabel.

choices.text: A picture of the text, drawn by JavaScript
choices.why: JavaScript describes the view; the platform draws its own widget.

choices.text: A Kotlin class generated when the app is built
choices.why: No Kotlin is generated per component; React Native creates the platform's widget while the app runs.

prompt: Why does a testID make it easier to run one suite on the Android and the iOS builds of a React Native app?
hint: Lesson 15 named the problem; who writes the name here?

choices.text: Because both platforms use resource ids
choices.why: iOS has no resource ids; testID becomes its accessibility identifier.

choices.text: Because Detox translates Android ids into iOS ones
choices.why: Nothing translates; one name is written once and each platform receives it.

choices.text: One name is written once and reaches both
choices.why: Right. It becomes the resource id on Android and the accessibility identifier on iOS.

choices.text: Because a testID is also the text a person reads
choices.why: A testID is never shown; it is a handle, not a label.

prompt: Your team already drives the Kotlin Tickets with Appium. Can the same Appium suite approach drive a React Native app, and what does it miss?
hint: What does the accessibility tree of a React Native app look like?

choices.text: No: Appium only drives apps written in Kotlin or Swift
choices.why: Appium sees native views, and React Native draws native views.

choices.text: Yes, but it cannot see the JavaScript side's work
choices.why: Right. The views are native, but the waiting has to be explicit, which is what Detox removes.

choices.text: Yes, and it misses nothing that Detox would see
choices.why: Detox sees timers, requests and the JavaScript thread from inside; Appium sees only the screen.

choices.text: Only through a web view context, since the app is a page
choices.why: There is no page; a React Native app has no HTML to switch into.

prompt: Which of these keep a React Native app busy in Detox's eyes?
hint: The table of section 03.

choices.text: A fetch to boxoffice still waiting for its answer
choices.why: Right. A request in flight is work Detox waits for.

choices.text: A setTimeout about to fire
choices.why: Right. A pending JavaScript timer counts.

choices.text: boxoffice writing to its log
choices.why: boxoffice is another program on your computer; Detox watches the app.

choices.text: The spec's own fetch to localhost:8080
choices.why: The spec runs in Node on the computer, outside the app; its requests are not the app's work.

prompt: Lesson 16 needed an idling resource for Tickets's load. Why does the React Native list need nothing of the kind?
hint: What does Detox watch that Espresso does not?

choices.text: Because fetch runs on the main thread in React Native
choices.why: Network work never runs on the main thread; Detox watches requests in flight directly.

choices.text: Because the list loads faster than Espresso can look
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; a slow load would be waited for too.

choices.text: Detox counts network requests as busy
choices.why: Right. The request keeps the app busy until its answer is in and the list is drawn.

choices.text: Because Detox sleeps two seconds before each step
choices.why: Detox never sleeps a fixed time; it waits for idleness.

prompt: Match each tool to the way it waits for the app.
hint: The comparison table of section 03.

pairs.right: the test waits explicitly, element by element
it waits for the main thread, plus idling resources
it waits until the app is idle in every way it watches

right_distractors: it sleeps a fixed time before each step

prompt: On Android, what is Detox built on?
hint: Section 03 says it is closer to one of the lesson 15 and 16 tools.

choices.text: Appium's UiAutomator2 driver
choices.why: Detox does not drive from outside; it lives in the app.

choices.text: Espresso, inside the app
choices.why: Right. Its library in the app uses Espresso and talks to the test over a WebSocket.

choices.text: A web view that hosts the JavaScript
choices.why: There is no web view in a React Native app.

choices.text: adb shell input commands
choices.why: Those tap coordinates blindly; Detox acts on views it can see.

prompt: Which three files did npx detox init write?
hint: The capture lists them.

choices.text: package.json, App.tsx and index.js
choices.why: Those came from the React Native template, not from Detox.

choices.text: build.gradle, DetoxTest.java and .detoxrc.js
choices.why: The Android changes are made by hand from the guide; init writes none of them.

choices.text: .detoxrc.js, e2e/jest.config.js and e2e/starter.test.js
choices.why: Right. The configuration, Jest's settings for the specs, and an example spec.

choices.text: jest.config.js, __tests__ and tsconfig.json
choices.why: Those are the template's own unit test and TypeScript settings.

prompt: A Detox run of the debug build installs the APK, opens the app, and the app shows a red error about not reaching the development server. What was forgotten?
hint: Where does a debug build get its JavaScript?

choices.text: Metro: npx react-native start
choices.why: Right. A debug build loads its JavaScript from Metro on the computer, reached through reversePorts 8081.

choices.text: Starting boxoffice before the test
choices.why: boxoffice serves the shows; the development server is Metro, which serves the app's code.

choices.text: Running npx detox init a second time
choices.why: init writes files once; it starts no server.

choices.text: Deleting e2e/starter.test.js
choices.why: A leftover example spec fails on its own ids; it does not stop the app loading.

prompt: Which port does .detoxrc.js reverse for Metro?
hint: reversePorts.

prompt: Put the setup of section 04 in order.
hint: Detox goes into a project that has to exist first.
items: create the project with the React Native command line
install detox into tickets-rn as a dev dependency
replace .detoxrc.js with the Android emulator configuration
make the Android changes from Detox's guide and run npx detox build

prompt: Why does the spec fetch sh-103 from localhost:8080, while the app asks 10.0.2.2:8080?
hint: Where does each one run?

choices.text: Because boxoffice listens on two addresses
choices.why: It is one boxoffice; the two names reach it from two places.

choices.text: The spec runs on the computer, the app on the emulator
choices.why: Right. On the computer boxoffice is localhost; from the emulator it is 10.0.2.2 (lesson 14).

choices.text: Because Detox forwards localhost into the emulator
choices.why: reversePorts forwards 8081 for Metro; it does not change where the spec runs.

choices.text: So that the spec's request does not keep the app busy
choices.why: The spec's request is outside the app either way; the address follows where the code runs.

prompt: The spec checks the error line with not.toExist(), where lesson 16 checked Tickets's banner with not(isDisplayed()). Why the difference?
hint: How does each app hide the element?

choices.text: Detox has no isDisplayed matcher
choices.why: Detox has toBeVisible and not.toBeVisible; the choice follows the app, not the tool.

choices.text: React Native hides every view it does not need
choices.why: It renders exactly what the component returns; the error line is left out by the code, on purpose.

choices.text: The line is left out of the tree, not hidden
choices.why: Right. failed && <Text…> renders nothing on a good load, while Tickets's layout always has the banner.

choices.text: not.toExist is faster on a slow emulator
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; each check matches how the element is hidden.

prompt: npx detox test -c android.emu.debug failed on the recording machine before any test ran. What did it refuse?
hint: Read the DetoxRuntimeError.

choices.text: The spec, for a syntax error
choices.why: Jest never reached the spec's tests; Tests: 0 total.

choices.text: Booting the Pixel_8_API_35 emulator
choices.why: Right. No AVD of that name exists there, and the list of available ones was empty.

choices.text: Installing an APK that was never built
choices.why: It failed before reaching the APK, at choosing a device.

choices.text: Connecting to Metro on port 8081
choices.why: No app ran, so nothing asked Metro for anything.

prompt: To start the app fresh, killing any copy an earlier spec left running, the spec calls device.launchApp({ ___: true }).
hint: A new one.

prompt: The list now asks boxoffice again every second, and every Detox spec times out on its first expect, though the screen looks right. Why?
hint: When does Detox act?

choices.text: The second request breaks the first one's answer
choices.why: Each request answers normally; the screen is right.

choices.text: The app is never idle
choices.why: Right. Detox acts only on an idle app, and this one never is.

choices.text: boxoffice refuses more than one request a second
choices.why: boxoffice has no rate limit; it answers every one.

choices.text: setInterval is forbidden in React Native
choices.why: It is ordinary JavaScript and works; it just never stops.

prompt: Of the three ways out of a polling app, why does the lesson rank making the app quiet in the test build above device.setURLBlacklist?
hint: What does the blacklist cover, and what does it leave?

choices.text: Because setURLBlacklist does not exist in Detox 20
choices.why: It exists; the issue is what it covers.

choices.text: Because ignoring an address makes tests slower
choices.why: It makes them faster, if anything; the problem is the timer it leaves.

choices.text: Because the blacklist switches synchronisation off entirely
choices.why: It removes only matching requests; the rest stays on, which is why it beats disabling.

choices.text: The timer would still keep the app busy
choices.why: Right. A quiet test build removes both, and the spec keeps full synchronisation.

prompt: Why is device.enableSynchronization() in a finally block in the lesson's spec?
hint: What if a waitFor fails?

choices.text: So a failure cannot leave later specs without synchronisation
choices.why: Right. Without it, every later spec in the file would run unsynchronised and fail or pass for the wrong reasons.

choices.text: Because Detox refuses to disable synchronisation outside a try
choices.why: Detox imposes no such rule; the finally is for the test's own safety.

choices.text: To make the waitFor calls retry
choices.why: waitFor retries by itself until its timeout; finally only runs at the end.

choices.text: Because the app stops polling when synchronisation is on
choices.why: Synchronisation changes how Detox waits, not what the app does.

prompt: A Detox spec that passed for months now waits two minutes and fails on every run since a release added a pulsing live badge to the list. The badge looks fine. Where do you look first?
hint: Which row of the table does a pulsing badge keep true?

choices.text: At the badge's testID, which may be missing
choices.why: A missing id would fail the step that looks for it, not every step after a two-minute wait.

choices.text: At the animation, which keeps the app busy
choices.why: Right. A looping animation means the app is never idle; Detox's busy list would name it.

choices.text: At boxoffice's logs, for slow answers
choices.why: A slow answer ends; this wait never does, and it began with the badge.

choices.text: At the emulator, which may need more memory
choices.why: Memory would not appear exactly with a release that added an animation.

prompt: Match each Tickets situation to how the test of lessons 15 to 17 waits for it.
hint: Outside, inside with the main thread, inside with everything.

pairs.left: the list loading, driven by Appium
the list loading on Tickets's own thread, in Espresso
the React Native list loading, in Detox
pairs.right: nothing: the request keeps the app busy

pairs.left: the React Native list polling every second, in Detox
pairs.right: waitFor with a timeout, synchronisation off

right_distractors: a fixed sleep long enough for the slowest device

prompt: A teammate proposes calling device.disableSynchronization() in beforeAll, for every spec, because one spec hung once. What is the cost?
hint: What did synchronisation do for the spec of section 05?

choices.text: None; Detox waits just the same without it
choices.why: Without it Detox waits for nothing, and a plain expect looks once.

choices.text: The app stops loading its shows
choices.why: The app behaves the same; only the test's waiting changes.

choices.text: Every spec now needs explicit waits
choices.why: Right. It throws away Detox's one idea for all specs to fix one; switch it off only where the app never settles.

choices.text: Detox can no longer find elements by testID
choices.why: Finding is unaffected; only waiting is.
